content.narrative_summary: The NYHA classification is a clinician‐assessed functional categorization of symptoms and functional capacity in patients with symptomatic (stage C) or advanced (stage D) heart failure, serving as an independent predictor of mortality and guiding treatment eligibility. Although reproducibility can be limited, it is widely used at baseline and throughout follow-up; patients with improving symptoms remain categorized by their highest stage (eg, a patient with stage C HF who becomes asymptomatic remains stage C).

section_headings: 2.2. Classification of HF by Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF)
content.narrative_summary: This section describes the importance of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in classifying heart failure (HF) into reduced (HFrEF, LVEF ≤40%), preserved (HFpEF, LVEF ≥50%), and mildly reduced or mid-range (HFmrEF, LVEF 41–49%) categories. It notes that clinical trials typically enroll patients with reduced LVEF, and that terminology for recovered or improved EF has been avoided in favor of ‘HF with improved EF’ (HFimpEF). The section highlights the dynamic nature of LVEF over time, the need for objective measures to support diagnosis, and the prognostic significance of LVEF trajectory.

section_headings: Trends in Mortality and Hospitalization for HF
Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Mortality and Hospitalization for HF
content.narrative_summary: Heart failure (HF) is an increasing health and economic burden in the United States, with age-adjusted death rates rising from 275,000 deaths in 2009 to 310,000 in 2014. U.S. hospitalizations for HF fell until 2012 but then rose by 26% from 2013 to 2017, reaching 1.2 million admissions in 2017. Among Medicare beneficiaries, HF incidence declined from 36 cases per 1000 in 2011 to 27 per 1000 in 2014 and stabilized through 2016; incidence of HFrEF decreased while HFpEF increased. Deaths from cardiomyopathies have increased due to improved recognition and documentation. Racial and ethnic disparities persist, with non-Hispanic Black patients experiencing the highest HF mortality rates (~92 per 100,000 vs. 87 per 100,000 for non-Hispanic White patients).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Clinical Assessment: History and Physical Examination

rows.recommendation: In patients with HF, vital signs and evidence of clinical congestion should be assessed at each encounter to guide overall management, including adjustment of diuretics and other medications (1-6).
In patients with symptomatic HF, clinical factors indicating the presence of advanced HF should be sought via the history and physical examination (7-12).
In patients with cardiomyopathy, a 3-generation family history should be obtained or updated when assessing the cause of the cardiomyopathy to identify possible inherited disease (13,14).
In patients presenting with HF, a thorough history and physical examination should direct diagnostic strategies to uncover specific causes that may warrant disease-specific management (15,16).

In patients presenting with HF, a thorough history and physical examination should be obtained and performed to identify cardiac and noncardiac disorders, lifestyle and behavioral factors, and social determinants of health that might cause or accelerate the development or progression of HF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Use of Biomarkers for Prevention, Initial Diagnosis, and Risk Stratification

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients presenting with dyspnea, measurement of B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal prohormone of B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is useful to support a diagnosis or exclusion of HF (1-12).
2. In patients with chronic HF, measurements of BNP or NT-proBNP levels are recommended for risk stratification (11,13-29).
3. In patients hospitalized for HF, measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP levels at admission is recommended to establish prognosis (11,13-19).

4. In patients at risk of developing HF, BNP or NT-proBNP-based screening followed by team-based care, including a cardiovascular specialist, can be useful to prevent the development of LV dysfunction or new-onset HF (30,31).
5. In patients hospitalized for HF, a predischarge BNP or NT-proBNP level can be useful to inform the trajectory of the patient and establish a postdischarge prognosis (14,17,20-29).

content.narrative_summary: This section discusses that BNP and NT-proBNP have higher sensitivity than specificity for ruling out heart failure, and elevated levels occur in both cardiac and noncardiac conditions. Higher biomarker levels predict adverse short- and long-term outcomes, including all-cause and cardiovascular death and major events. The STOP-HF trial demonstrated that BNP-based screening reduced incident asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction and related events. Predischarge BNP and NT-proBNP levels are strong predictors of death or hospital readmission, though targeting specific thresholds has not consistently improved outcomes; changes in these biomarkers may guide prognosis and optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy.

content.title: 4.3 Genetic Evaluation and Testing
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis outlines that when a genetic or inherited cardiomyopathy is suspected, a three‐generation family pedigree should be obtained. Genetic variants are implicated in 25–40% of DCM with family history and 10–30% without. Phenotype and family history guide clinically actionable genetic testing, aiding risk stratification and management decisions including ICD implantation and exercise restriction. Counseling before and after testing helps patients understand implications for themselves and relatives. The supportive text describes pathogenic variants in titin, lamin A/C, desmosomal proteins, and filamin-C associated with various cardiomyopathy phenotypes and arrhythmia risks. Identification of these variants may prompt primary prevention ICDs and exercise advice. Genetic confirmation of Fabry disease indicates enzyme replacement or migalastat therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Genetic Evaluation and Testing

rows.recommendation: In first-degree relatives of selected patients with genetic or inherited cardiomyopathies, genetic screening and counseling are recommended to detect cardiac disease and prompt consideration of treatments to decrease HF progression and sudden death (1,2).
In select patients with nonischemic cardiomyopathy, referral for genetic counseling and testing is reasonable to identify conditions that could guide treatment for patients and family members (3,4).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Evaluation With Cardiac Imaging

rows.recommendation: In patients with suspected or new-onset HF, or those presenting with acute decompensated HF, a chest x-ray should be performed to assess heart size and pulmonary congestion and to detect alternative cardiac, pulmonary, and other diseases that may cause or contribute to the patient's symptoms (1,2).
In patients with suspected or newly diagnosed HF, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) should be performed during initial evaluation to assess cardiac structure and function (3).

In patients with HF who have had a significant clinical change, or who have received GDMT and are being considered for invasive procedures or device therapy, repeat measurement of EF, degree of structural remodeling, and valvular function are useful to inform therapeutic interventions (4-7).

In patients for whom echocardiography is inadequate, alternative imaging (e.g., cardiac magnetic resonance [CMR], cardiac computed tomography [CT], radionuclide imaging) is recommended for assessment of LVEF (8-15).
In patients with HF or cardiomyopathy, CMR can be useful for diagnosis or management (16-23).
In patients with HF, an evaluation for possible ischemic heart disease can be useful to identify the cause and guide management (24-27).

content.title: 4.5. Invasive Evaluation
content.narrative_summary: Invasive evaluation of patients with heart failure (HF) provides important information for determining the cause of HF and guiding treatment. Routine right-heart catheterization alone does not reliably guide therapy, but selective invasive hemodynamic monitoring is useful in patients with uncertain hemodynamics or persistent or worsening symptoms. Endomyocardial biopsy may be advantageous when a specific histological diagnosis (eg, amyloidosis or myocarditis) will influence management but carries procedural risks that preclude routine use. Recommendation-specific text details indications for biopsy in diagnostic evaluation and hemodynamic monitoring in management, and notes that routine monitoring or biopsy offers no benefit and may cause harm.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Invasive Evaluation

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with HF, endomyocardial biopsy may be useful when a specific diagnosis is suspected that would influence therapy (1,2).

2. In selected patients with HF with persistent or worsening symptoms, signs, diagnostic parameters, and in whom hemodynamics are uncertain, invasive hemodynamic monitoring can be useful to guide management.
3. In patients with HF, routine use of invasive hemodynamic monitoring is not recommended (3,4).
4. For patients undergoing routine evaluation of HF, endomyocardial biopsy should not be performed because of the risk of complications (5,6).

content.title: 4.6. Wearables and Remote Monitoring (Including Telemonitoring and Device Monitoring)
section_headings: 4.6. Wearables and Remote Monitoring (Including Telemonitoring and Device Monitoring)
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes HF as a chronic condition with high event rates despite in-person monitoring and outlines remote monitoring strategies tested in trials, including implantable PA pressure sensors (CardioMEMS), noninvasive telemonitoring, and monitoring via implanted devices (ICDs or CRT-Ds). Results from a randomized trial and observational studies support implantable sensors to reduce HF hospitalizations, but other trials failed primary endpoints. The value of noninvasive telemonitoring and monitoring of physiological parameters remains uncertain, and further study is needed. The supportive text summarizes the CHAMPION trial’s 28% reduction in HF hospitalizations with implanted PA monitors under stable GDMT, notes persistent LVEF benefit, trial nonblinding, and differential patient contact, and reviews cost-effectiveness analyses showing variable economic value dependent on clinical benefit magnitude and treatment duration.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for Wearables and Remote Monitoring (Including Telemonitoring and Device Monitoring)

rows.recommendation: 1. In selected adult patients with NYHA class III HF and history of a HF hospitalization in the past year or elevated natriuretic peptide levels, on maximally tolerated stable doses of GDMT with optimal device therapy, the usefulness of wireless monitoring of PA pressure by an implanted hemodynamic monitor to reduce the risk of subsequent HF hospitalizations is uncertain (1-4).
2. In patients with NYHA class III HF with a HF hospitalization within the previous year, wireless monitoring of the PA pressure by an implanted hemodynamic monitor provides uncertain value (4-7).

content.title: 4.7. Exercise and Functional Capacity Testing
section_headings: Recommendations for Exercise and Functional Capacity Testing
content.narrative_summary: Functional impairment and exercise intolerance are common in heart failure. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) and the 6-minute walk test are standardized, reliable, and reproducible measures of functional capacity. The NYHA functional classification (I–IV) grades the severity of symptoms and guides candidacy for treatments. CPET variables, including peak VO₂, are prognostic and used to stratify risk and timing for advanced HF therapies (e.g., transplant, LVAD). Patients on beta blockers may have adjusted peak VO₂ thresholds for transplant listing. The 6-minute walk test is a widely available, well-tolerated alternative to CPET.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Exercise and Functional Capacity Testing

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with HF, assessment and documentation of NYHA functional classification are recommended to determine eligibility for treatments (1-3).
2. In selected ambulatory patients with HF, cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is recommended to determine appropriateness of advanced treatments (e.g., LVAD, heart transplant) (4-8).
3. In ambulatory patients with HF, performing a CPET or 6-minute walk test is reasonable to assess functional capacity (4,5,9-16).
4. In ambulatory patients with unexplained dyspnea, CPET is reasonable to evaluate the cause of dyspnea (17,18).

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with hypertension, blood pressure should be controlled in accordance with GDMT for hypertension to prevent symptomatic HF (1-9).
2. In patients with type 2 diabetes and either established CVD or at high cardiovascular risk, SGLT2i should be used to prevent hospitalizations for HF (10-12).

3. In the general population, healthy lifestyle habits such as regular physical activity, maintaining normal weight, healthy dietary patterns, and avoiding smoking are helpful to reduce future risk of HF (13-21).

4. For patients at risk of developing HF, natriuretic peptide biomarker-based screening followed by team-based care, including a cardiovascular specialist optimizing GDMT, can be useful to prevent the development of LV dysfunction (systolic or diastolic) or new-onset HF (22,23).
5. In the general population, validated multivariable risk scores can be useful to estimate subsequent risk of incident HF (24-26).

content.title: 6. STAGE B (PATIENTS WITH PRE-HF)
section_headings: 6.1. Management of Stage B: Preventing the Syndrome of Clinical HF in Patients With Pre-HF
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis notes that stage B heart failure represents asymptomatic structural and functional cardiac abnormalities analogous to stage A risk factors, for which initial lifestyle modification and pharmacological therapies (such as renin–angiotensin system inhibitors and beta blockers) may prevent or delay progression to symptomatic HF. Comorbidities including diabetes, obesity, and hypertension are managed per current guidelines. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists have demonstrated benefit post–MI in symptomatic HF, while ARNi efficacy in stage B remains under study, with the PARADISE-MI trial results pending.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Management of Stage B: Preventing the Syndrome of Clinical HF in Patients With Pre-HF

rows.recommendation: In patients with LVEF ≤40%, ACEi should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and reduce mortality (1–4).
In patients with a recent or remote history of MI or ACS, statins should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and adverse cardiovascular events (5–9).
In patients with a recent MI and LVEF ≤40% who are intolerant to ACEi, ARB should be used to prevent symptomatic HF and reduce mortality (10).
In patients with a recent or remote history of MI or acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and LVEF ≤40%, evidence-based beta blockers should be used to reduce mortality (11–13).

In patients who are at least 40 days post–MI with LVEF ≤30% and NYHA class I symptoms while receiving GDMT and have reasonable expectation of meaningful survival for >1 year, an ICD is recommended for primary prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD) to reduce total mortality (14).
In patients with LVEF ≤40%, beta blockers should be used to prevent symptomatic HF (12,13).
In patients with LVEF ≤50%, thiazolidinediones should not be used because they increase the risk of HF, including hospitalizations (15).
In patients with LVEF ≤50%, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers with negative inotropic effects may be harmful (16,17).

content.narrative_summary: This section provides supporting evidence for earlier recommendations regarding post–myocardial infarction management and heart failure prevention: 1. ACE inhibitors reduce maladaptive remodeling, mortality, hospitalizations, and progression to severe HF in patients with reduced or asymptomatic LV dysfunction. 2. Statins prevent adverse coronary events and reduce incident HF and hospitalizations after MI or ACS. 3. ARBs (valsartan in VALIANT) are comparable to ACE inhibitors for mortality and cardiovascular outcomes post‐MI, though losartan in OPTIMAAL did not meet noninferiority; caution is advised due to angioedema risks. 4. Beta blockers improve remodeling and reduce mortality and hospitalizations in patients with reduced LVEF post‐MI, both symptomatic and asymptomatic, as shown in trials including SOLVD prevention and SAVE. 5. Beta blockers are recommended to prevent symptomatic HF in patients with reduced LVEF, including those without prior MI, based on SOLVD post hoc analyses. 7. Thiazolidinediones increase fluid retention and HF risk; pioglitazone and rosiglitazone worsened outcomes in diabetic patients with depressed LVEF.

section_headings: 7.2. Diuretics and Decongestion Strategies in Patients With HF
content.narrative_summary: This page continues discussion of exercise training in heart failure, noting modest reductions in all-cause mortality and improvements in functional capacity, exercise duration, quality of life, and HF hospitalizations from RCTs and meta-analyses. Formal cardiac rehabilitation programs combining medical evaluation, education, dietary recommendations, psychosocial support, and exercise training improve functional capacity, tolerance, and HF-specific outcomes. The synopsis describes diuretic mechanisms: loop diuretics act at the loop of Henle and are preferred in most HF patients; thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics act in the distal tubule, may be used in hypertension or mild fluid retention, and metolazone or chlorothiazide can be added for refractory edema. Diuretics should be titrated to eliminate fluid retention using the lowest effective dose; mortality effects are uncertain, so diuretics are combined with guideline-directed medical therapy. Hyponatremia is a complication of chronic diuretic use, and vasopressin antagonists may help in acute volume overload.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diuretics and Decongestion Strategies in Patients With HF

rows.recommendation: In patients with HF who have fluid retention, diuretics are recommended to relieve congestion, improve symptoms, and prevent worsening HF (1-5).

For patients with HF and congestive symptoms, addition of a thiazide (e.g., metolazone) to treatment with a loop diuretic should be reserved for patients who do not respond to moderate- or high-dose loop diuretics to minimize electrolyte abnormalities (6).

section_headings: 7.3.1. Renin-Angiotensin System Inhibition With ACEi or ARB or ARNi
content.narrative_summary: Following Table 12 summarizing commonly used loop and thiazide diuretics, the text discusses choice of loop diuretics for HF, noting furosemide as most common but others like bumetanide and torsemide may have better bioavailability. Outpatient dosing is initiated low and titrated by 0.5–1.0 mg/kg daily until decongestion; unresponsiveness may occur with high sodium intake, NSAIDs, or renal impairment. Diuretic resistance can be overcome by escalating dose, intravenous administration, or combining diuretic classes. Addition of thiazide‐like agents (eg, metolazone) enhances natriuresis but increases risks of electrolyte disturbances and renal dysfunction. High-dose IV loop diuretics did not worsen survival in the DOSE trial, supporting their use.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Renin-Angiotensin System Inhibition With ACEi or ARB or ARNi

rows.recommendation: In patients with HFrEF and NYHA class II to III symptoms, the use of ARNi is recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality (1-5).
In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF, the use of ACEi is beneficial to reduce morbidity and mortality when the use of ARNi is not feasible (6-13).

In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF who are intolerant to ACEi because of cough or angioedema and when the use of ARNi is not feasible, the use of ARB is recommended to reduce morbidity and mortality (14-18).
In patients with previous or current symptoms of chronic HFrEF, in whom ARNi is not feasible, treatment with an ACEi or ARB provides high economic value (19-25).

content.narrative_summary: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone or eplerenone) improve all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalizations, and sudden cardiac death in HFrEF patients. Contraindications include eGFR ≤30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or serum potassium ≥5.0 mEq/L. Eplerenone has fewer anti-androgen side effects than spironolactone. Initiate spironolactone or eplerenone at 25 mg daily (increasing to 50 mg as tolerated), reduce dose when eGFR is 30–49 mL/min/1.73 m2, and monitor potassium and renal function at 1 week, 4 weeks, then every 6 months. Economic analyses show high value with low cost per QALY.

Careful monitoring of potassium, renal function, and diuretic dosing should be performed at initiation and closely monitored thereafter to minimize risk of hyperkalemia and renal insufficiency (1–3).

3. In patients taking MRA whose serum potassium cannot be maintained at <5.5 mEq/L, MRA should be discontinued to avoid life-threatening hyperkalemia (8,9).

content.narrative_summary: This page provides recommendations for adjunctive drug treatments in heart failure, including omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation, use of potassium binders for hyperkalemia during RAASi therapy, and anticoagulation in patients with chronic HFrEF without specific indications. A synopsis of key trials and recommendation-specific supportive text reviewing studies such as GISSI-HF, REDUCE-IT, and PEARL-HF are presented.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Other Drug Treatment

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with HF class II to IV symptoms, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation may be reasonable to use as adjunctive therapy to reduce mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations (1-4).

2. In patients with HF who experience hyperkalemia (serum potassium level ≥5.5 mEq/L) while taking a renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitor (RAASi), the effectiveness of potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) to improve outcomes by facilitating continuation of RAASi therapy is uncertain (5,6).

3. In patients with chronic HFrEF without a specific indication (e.g., venous thromboembolism [VTE], AF, a previous thromboembolic event, or a cardioembolic source), anticoagulation is not recommended (7-9).

section_headings: 7.3.7. Drugs of Unproven Value or Drugs That May Worsen HF
content.narrative_summary: Continuation of the discussion on potassium binder trials in heart failure, including the HARMONIZE trial showing that sodium zirconium cyclosilicate maintains normokalemia versus placebo with noted adverse effects (hypomagnesemia, edema). Retrospective analyses found no reduction in thromboembolic events with warfarin in HF, and randomized trials comparing aspirin, warfarin, clopidogrel, and rivaroxaban in HFrEF without specific indications demonstrated no benefit and increased bleeding risk, supporting avoidance of anticoagulation absent a clear indication. A synopsis highlights that, despite strong evidence for some HFrEF treatments, multiple drug classes—including calcium channel blockers, antiarrhythmics, thiazolidinediones, DPP-4 inhibitors, NSAIDs, vitamins, hormones, and supplements—have unproven value or potential harm as outlined in Table 13.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Drugs of Unproven Value or Drugs That May Worsen HF

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with HFrEF, dihydropyridine calcium channel-blocking drugs are not recommended treatment for HF (1,2).
2. In patients with HFrEF, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and hormonal therapy are not recommended other than to correct specific deficiencies (3-9).
3. In patients with HFrEF, nondihydropyridine calcium channel-blocking drugs are not recommended (10-13).
4. In patients with HFrEF, class IC antiarrhythmic medications and dronedarone may increase the risk of mortality (14-16).
5. In patients with HFrEF, thiazolidinediones increase the risk of worsening HF symptoms and hospitalizations (17-21).

6. In patients with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors saxagliptin and alogliptin increase the risk of HF hospitalization and should be avoided in patients with HF (22-24).
7. In patients with HFrEF, NSAIDs worsen HF symptoms and should be avoided or withdrawn whenever possible (25-28).

content.title: Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text
content.narrative_summary:
1. Second-generation dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, amlodipine, felodipine) are more selective for vascular smooth muscle, reduce afterload, and may benefit chronic HF. PRAISE-1 showed reduced mortality in nonischemic cardiomyopathy; PRAISE-2 showed no survival benefit. They may be used to treat hypertension in HF patients with elevated blood pressure despite GDMT.
2. Nutritional supplements and hormonal therapies (eg, vitamins D, thiamine; carnitine; taurine; coenzyme Q10; testosterone; growth hormone; thyroid hormone) have limited evidence. The largest RCT of coenzyme Q10 (Q-SYMBIO) showed no change in NYHA class but reduced major cardiovascular events at 2 years. Hormonal therapies have generally neutral effects on HF outcomes.
3. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are myocardial depressants, poorly tolerated in HF. Verapamil had no impact on survival or major events post-MI; diltiazem was associated with higher recurrent HF risk after acute MI.
4. Class I antiarrhythmics in asymptomatic post-MI patients (CAST) increased mortality. Class IC and III agents are generally avoided in structural heart disease. Amiodarone and dofetilide have neutral mortality effects in HFrEF. Class IA/IB agents are unstudied but may be considered for refractory ventricular arrhythmias with electrophysiology consultation.
5. Thiazolidinediones (PPAR-γ agonists) increase insulin sensitivity and sodium reabsorption, leading to fluid retention. Observational studies, meta-analyses, and clinical trials associate them with increased HF incidence or events in patients with or without prior HF.
6. DPP-4 inhibitors (eg, saxagliptin, alogliptin) affect glucose homeostasis through multiple mechanisms. Saxagliptin and alogliptin have been associated with increased HF hospitalization risk, but…

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for GDMT Dosing: Sequencing and Uptitration

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with HFrEF, titration of guideline-directed medication dosing to achieve target doses showed to be efficacious in RCTs is recommended, to reduce cardiovascular mortality and HF hospitalizations, unless not well tolerated (1-10).

2. In patients with HFrEF, titration and optimization of guideline-directed medications as frequently as every 1 to 2 weeks depending on the patient’s symptoms, vital signs, and laboratory findings can be useful to optimize management.

content.title: 7.3.9. Additional Medical Therapies
section_headings: 7.3.9.1. Management of Stage C HF: Ivabradine
7.3.9.2. Pharmacological Treatment for Stage C HFrEF: Digoxin
content.narrative_summary: The SHIFT trial demonstrated that reducing heart rate with ivabradine, a sinoatrial node If current inhibitor, lowers the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization in patients with symptomatic HFrEF (LVEF ≤35%) in sinus rhythm with resting heart rate ≥70 bpm already on maximally tolerated beta-blocker therapy. Although only a quarter of SHIFT patients were on optimal beta-blocker doses, ivabradine provided benefit after GDMT optimization. For digoxin, one large RCT in NYHA class II–III HFrEF showed modest reductions in combined mortality and hospitalization but no mortality benefit; retrospective analyses suggest improvements in symptoms and exercise tolerance. Use of digoxin in contemporary GDMT is reserved for patients who remain symptomatic despite guideline-directed therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for the Management of Stage C HF: Ivabradine

rows.recommendation: For patients with symptomatic (NYHA class II to III) stable chronic HFrEF (LVEF ≤35%) who are receiving GDMT, including a beta blocker at maximum tolerated dose, and who are in sinus rhythm with a heart rate of ≥70 bpm at rest, ivabradine can be beneficial to reduce HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death (1,2).

content.narrative_summary: The top of the page continues a discussion of digoxin in heart failure, noting that higher serum concentrations (≥1.2 ng/mL and ≥1.6 ng/mL) are associated with increased mortality, that digoxin should be optimized on guideline-directed medical therapy before adding it, and that withdrawal may worsen clinical status. Digoxin is usually initiated at 0.125–0.25 mg daily (lower doses in patients >70 years, with renal impairment, or low body mass), with higher doses rarely needed. The page then introduces soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) stimulators, presenting a Class 2b, Level B-R recommendation for vericiguat to reduce heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular death in selected high-risk HFrEF patients on GDMT with recent worsening. The Synopsis summarizes the VICTORIA trial design and mechanistic rationale of vericiguat, and the Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text details inclusion criteria (LVEF <45%, NYHA II–IV, elevated natriuretic peptides, recent HF worsening) and primary and secondary outcomes, including relative risk reductions and subgroup findings.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for Pharmacological Treatment for Stage C HFrEF: Soluble Guanylyl Cyclase Stimulators

rows.recommendation: In selected high-risk patients with HFrEF and recent worsening of HF already on GDMT, an oral soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator (vericiguat) may be considered to reduce HF hospitalization and cardiovascular death (1).

content.narrative_summary: This section introduces device and interventional therapies for HFrEF and outlines recommendations for ICD and CRT therapy, noting that referenced studies are summarized in the Online Data Supplements.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for ICDs and CRTs

rows.recommendation: In patients with nonischemic DCM or ischemic heart disease at least 40 days post-MI with LVEF ≤35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms on chronic GDMT, who have reasonable expectation of meaningful survival for >1 year, ICD therapy is recommended for primary prevention of SCD to reduce total mortality (1-9).

In patients at least 40 days post-MI with LVEF ≤30% and NYHA class I symptoms while receiving GDMT, who have reasonable expectation of meaningful survival for >1 year, ICD therapy is recommended for primary prevention of SCD to reduce total mortality (6).

For patients who have LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, a non-LBBB pattern with a QRS duration ≥150 ms, and NYHA class II, III, or ambulatory class IV symptoms on GDMT, CRT can be useful to reduce total mortality, reduce hospitalizations, and improve symptoms and QOL.
In patients with high-degree or complete heart block and LVEF of 36% to 50%, CRT is reasonable to reduce total mortality, reduce hospitalizations, and improve symptoms and QOL.

For patients who have LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB with a QRS duration of 120 to 149 ms, and NYHA class II, III, or ambulatory IV symptoms on GDMT, CRT can be useful to reduce total mortality, reduce hospitalizations, and improve symptoms and QOL.

In patients with AF and LVEF ≤35% on GDMT, CRT can be useful to reduce total mortality, improve symptoms and QOL, and increase LVEF, if: a) the patient requires ventricular pacing or otherwise meets CRT criteria and b) atrioventricular nodal ablation or pharmacological rate control will allow near 100% ventricular pacing with CRT.

For patients on GDMT who have LVEF ≤35% and are undergoing placement of a new or replacement device implantation with anticipated requirement for significant (>40%) ventricular pacing, CRT can be useful to reduce total mortality, reduce hospitalizations, and improve symptoms and QOL.
In patients with genetic arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with high-risk features of sudden death, with EF ≤45%, implantation of ICD is reasonable to decrease sudden death.

For patients who have LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, a non-LBBB pattern with QRS duration of 120 to 149 ms, and NYHA class III or ambulatory class IV on GDMT, CRT may be considered to reduce total mortality, reduce hospitalizations, and improve symptoms and QOL.

For patients who have LVEF ≤30%, ischemic cause of HF, sinus rhythm, LBBB with a QRS duration ≥150 ms, and NYHA class I symptoms on GDMT, CRT may be considered to reduce hospitalizations and improve symptoms and QOL.
In patients with QRS duration <120 ms, CRT is not recommended.
For patients with NYHA class I or II symptoms and non-LBBB pattern with QRS duration <150 ms, CRT is not recommended.
For patients whose comorbidities or frailty limit survival with good functional capacity to <1 year, ICD and cardiac resynchronization therapy with defibrillation (CRT-D) are not indicated.

content.title: Valvular Heart Disease
content.narrative_summary: This section outlines the management of valvular heart disease (VHD) in heart failure. The synopsis emphasizes that guideline‐directed medical therapy (GDMT) applies to all HFrEF patients, regardless of VHD, and recommends multidisciplinary evaluation per VHD guidelines. In mitral regurgitation, optimization of GDMT and careful reassessment before intervention—supported by COAPT and MITRA‐FR trial results—is important, with patient selection guided by echocardiographic and hemodynamic criteria. The aortic stenosis subsection discusses shared decision‐making between transcatheter and surgical valve replacement, ongoing TAVR UNLOAD trial evaluation, and continuation of GDMT. Tricuspid regurgitation focuses on its dynamic nature related to RV function and pulmonary hypertension, underlying cause management, and referral for intervention. The recommendation‐specific supportive text reinforces multidisciplinary team management to prevent HF worsening and adverse outcomes.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Valvular Heart Disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with HF, VHD should be managed in a multidisciplinary manner in accordance with clinical practice guidelines for VHD to prevent worsening of HF and adverse clinical outcomes (1–11).
In patients with chronic severe secondary MR and HFrEF, optimization of GDMT is recommended before any intervention for secondary MR related to LV dysfunction (3–5,12–14).

content.narrative_summary: This section discusses guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and secondary mitral regurgitation (MR). GDMT—including RAAS inhibition, beta-blockers, and biventricular pacing—improves MR and left ventricular (LV) dimensions. In a small RCT, sacubitril-valsartan significantly reduced effective regurgitant area and volume versus valsartan. The COAPT trial demonstrated a mortality benefit of transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) in patients with severe secondary MR, LVEF 20–50%, LVESD ≤70 mm, pulmonary artery systolic pressure ≤70 mm Hg, and persistent NYHA class II–IV symptoms on optimal GDMT. A heart failure cardiologist should optimize GDMT and ensure medical therapies are fully applied before considering valve intervention.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: FIGURE 10
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Treatment Approach in Secondary Mitral Regurgitation
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Flowchart for managing secondary mitral regurgitation: start with GDMT supervised by an HF specialist; in severe stage D MR (RVol ≥60 mL, RF ≥50%, ERO ≥0.40 cm²) assess LVEF. If LVEF ≥50% and severe persistent symptoms on optimal GDMT and AF therapy, proceed to MV surgery (Class 2b). If LVEF <50% with persistent symptoms on GDMT and favorable mitral anatomy (LVEF 20–50%; LVESD ≤70 mm; PASP ≤70 mm Hg), proceed to transcatheter edge-to-edge MV repair (Class 2a); if anatomy not favorable but severe symptoms persist, proceed to MV surgery (Class 2b). For patients undergoing CABG, consider concomitant MV surgery (Class 2b) or chordal-sparing MV replacement (Class 2a).

content.title: 7.6. Heart Failure With Mildly Reduced EF (HFmrEF) and Improved EF (HFimpHF); 7.6.1. HF With Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction
section_headings: Recommendations for HF With Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction
content.narrative_summary: The narrative notes the absence of prospective RCTs in patients with HFmrEF (LVEF 41%–49%), drawing on post hoc analyses of HFrEF trials to suggest that patients, especially those at the lower end of the LVEF spectrum, respond to guideline-directed medical therapies similarly to HFrEF. It recommends repeat LVEF evaluation to track disease trajectory and calls for future prospective studies. The recommendation-specific supportive text describes the EMPEROR-Preserved trial of empagliflozin, which showed a 21% reduction in the composite of HF hospitalization or cardiovascular death driven by a 29% reduction in HF hospitalizations, with benefits irrespective of diabetes status and in the LVEF 41%–49% subgroup.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for HF With Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with HFmrEF, SGLT2i can be beneficial in decreasing HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular mortality (1).

2. Among patients with current or previous symptomatic HFmrEF (LVEF, 41%–49%), use of evidence-based beta blockers for HFrEF, ARNi, ACEi, or ARB, and MRAs may be considered to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality, particularly among patients with LVEF on the lower end of this spectrum (2-9).

content.title: 7.6.2. HF With Improved Ejection Fraction
content.narrative_summary: Post hoc analyses of HFrEF trials including patients with HFmrEF (LVEF 41%–49%) show that GDMT—beta-blockers, ARNi, ACEi/ARB, and spironolactone—reduces all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, HF hospitalizations, and recurrent events. In HFmrEF, spironolactone is preferred for hypertension, and continuation of GDMT after LVEF improvement reduces relapse. Meta-analyses highlight heterogeneity in response, and patients with HFmrEF should have repeat LVEF evaluation and testing for disease-specific conditions (e.g., CAD, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis). The synopsis notes that although GDMT can improve symptoms, LVEF, and biomarkers in HFimpEF, structural abnormalities and symptoms often persist or recur when therapy is withdrawn, indicating remission rather than cure and the need for ongoing, optimized treatment even in asymptomatic or non-improving patients.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for HF With Improved Ejection Fraction

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with HFimpEF after treatment, GDMT should be continued to prevent relapse of HF and LV dysfunction, even in patients who may become asymptomatic (1).

content.title: Recommendations for HF With Preserved Ejection Fraction
content.narrative_summary: The page continues results of HF medication withdrawal showing reduced LVEF, worsened patient-reported outcomes, and changes in NT-proBNP and LV volumes. It introduces HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%) as a heterogenous syndrome affecting up to 50% of HF patients, associated with comorbidities such as hypertension, diabetes, obesity, CAD, CKD, and specific causes like amyloidosis. Past trials used variable definitions and showed limited mortality benefit. Current management highlights diuretics for congestion and symptom relief, with further nonpharmacological and diuretic guidance in Sections 7.1 and 7.2. The supportive text begins by reinforcing the role of intensive blood pressure control in reducing HF onset and adverse cardiovascular outcomes.

In patients with HFpEF, management of AF can be useful to improve symptoms.
In selected patients with HFpEF, MRAs may be considered to decrease hospitalizations, particularly among patients with LVEF on the lower end of this spectrum (5–7).
In selected patients with HFpEF, the use of ARB may be considered to decrease hospitalizations, particularly among patients with LVEF on the lower end of this spectrum (8,9).
In selected patients with HFpEF, ARNi may be considered to decrease hospitalizations, particularly among patients with LVEF on the lower end of this spectrum (10,11).
In patients with HFpEF, routine use of nitrates or phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors to increase activity or QOL is ineffective (12,13).

content.title: 7.8. Cardiac Amyloidosis; 7.8.1. Diagnosis of Cardiac Amyloidosis
content.narrative_summary: Cardiac amyloidosis is described as a restrictive cardiomyopathy due to deposition of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL-CM) or transthyretin (ATTR-CM). ATTR may be hereditary (ATTRv) due to pathogenic variants in the transthyretin gene (TTR) or wild-type. Diagnosis integrates clinical suspicion with imaging, laboratory testing, bone scintigraphy, and genetic testing. A diagnostic approach is outlined in Figure 13. Specific supportive text details criteria for LV wall thickness, preferred use of immunofixation electrophoresis to rule out AL-CM, use of technetium-based bone scans for ATTR-CM, and the role of TTR gene sequencing to distinguish hereditary from wild-type disease.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnosis of Cardiac Amyloidosis

rows.recommendation: Patients for whom there is a clinical suspicion for cardiac amyloidosis* (1–5) should have screening for serum and urine monoclonal light chains with serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis and serum free light chains (6).
rows.supporting_text: *LV wall thickness ≥14 mm in conjunction with fatigue, dyspnea, or edema, especially in the context of discordance between wall thickness on echocardiogram and QRS voltage on ECG, and in the context of aortic stenosis, HFpEF, carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, and autonomic or sensory polyneuropathy.

rows.recommendation: In patients with high clinical suspicion for cardiac amyloidosis, without evidence of serum or urine monoclonal light chains, bone scintigraphy should be performed to confirm the presence of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (7).

In patients for whom a diagnosis of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis is made, genetic testing with TTR gene sequencing is recommended to differentiate hereditary variant from wild-type transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (8).

content.title: Treatment of Cardiac Amyloidosis
section_headings: Recommendations for Treatment of Cardiac Amyloidosis
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis describes challenges in managing ATTR-CM patients with reduced ejection fraction, noting that GDMT may be poorly tolerated and that vasodilators and beta-blockers require careful use. It outlines disease-modifying therapies including TTR silencers (inotersen, patisiran), stabilizers (diflunisal, tafamidis), and tissue-clearance agents (doxycycline, TUDCA, EGCG). AL amyloidosis requires hematology-oncology referral. Ongoing trials of mRNA inhibitors and degraders are noted, with limited benefit observed for some agents. The Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text explains that tafamidis is currently the only therapy shown to improve cardiovascular outcomes in ATTR-CM by binding TTR, and begins cost-effectiveness data from the ATTR-ACT trial showing tafamidis adds survival and QALY but at low economic value.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Treatment of Cardiac Amyloidosis

rows.recommendation: In select patients with wild-type or variant transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis and NYHA class I to III HF symptoms, transthyretin tetramer stabilizer therapy (tafamidis) is indicated to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality (1).
At 2020 list prices, tafamidis provides low economic value (>$180,000 per QALY gained) in patients with HF with wild-type or variant transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (2).

In patients with cardiac amyloidosis and AF, anticoagulation is reasonable to reduce the risk of stroke regardless of the CHA2DS2-VASc (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 years, diabetes mellitus, stroke or transient ischemic attack [TIA], vascular disease, age 65 to 74 years, sex category) score (3,4).

content.narrative_summary: Table 16 provides criteria for defining advanced heart failure, indicating all four criteria must be present despite optimal guideline-directed treatment. Criteria include: (1) severe, persistent HF symptoms (NYHA class III [advanced] or IV); (2) severe cardiac dysfunction (one or more of LVEF ≤30%, isolated RV failure, nonoperable severe valve abnormalities, nonoperable severe congenital heart disease, or EF ≥40% with elevated natriuretic peptides and significant diastolic dysfunction); (3) hospitalizations or unplanned visits in the past 12 months for congestion requiring high-dose IV diuretics or combinations, low output requiring inotropes/vasoactive medications, or malignant arrhythmias; and (4) severe impairment of exercise capacity (inability to exercise or <300 m on 6-minute walk test or peak VO₂ <12–14 mL/kg/min). A footnote notes that criteria 1 and 4 may be met in patients with substantial limitations from other conditions, potentially limiting therapeutic options.

rows.recommendation: In patients with advanced (stage D) HF refractory to GDMT and device therapy who are eligible for and awaiting MCS or cardiac transplantation, continuous intravenous inotropic support is reasonable as “bridge therapy” (1-4).

content.title: 8.4. Mechanical Circulatory Support
content.narrative_summary: MCS is a therapeutic option for patients with advanced HFrEF to prolong life and improve functional capacity. Temporary and durable devices vary by implant location, approach, flow characteristics, pump mechanism, and ventricle(s) supported. Durable MCS is most appropriate for HFrEF with a dilated ventricle. All MCS devices will eventually be turned off for explant, recovery, or patient choice, and discussions should address discontinuation or escalation of support. Durable and destination therapy MCS provides survival and QOL benefits but carries risks including external electrical power tethering, rehospitalization, and complications from anticoagulation or high venous pressures. Thorough evaluation and multidisciplinary patient selection are essential.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Mechanical Circulatory Support

rows.recommendation: 1. In select patients with advanced HFrEF with NYHA class IV symptoms who are deemed to be dependent on continuous intravenous inotropes or temporary MCS, durable LVAD implantation is effective to improve functional status, QOL, and survival (1-18).

2. In select patients with advanced HFrEF who have NYHA class IV symptoms despite GDMT, durable MCS can be beneficial to improve symptoms, improve functional class, and reduce mortality (2,4,7,10,12-17,19).
3. In patients with advanced HFrEF who have NYHA class IV symptoms despite GDMT, durable MCS devices provide low to intermediate economic value based on current costs and outcomes (20-24).

4. In patients with advanced HFrEF and hemodynamic compromise and shock, temporary MCS, including percutaneous and extracorporeal ventricular assist devices, are reasonable as a “bridge to recovery” or “bridge to decision” (25-29).

9.1 Assessment of Patients Hospitalized With Decompensated HF
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis discusses initial triage of hemodynamic status in decompensated HF, emphasizing assessment of congestion, perfusion, and precipitating factors (including ischemia, arrhythmias, and ACS), involvement of a multidisciplinary team, and urgent management of pulmonary edema or severe hypertension. Recommendation-specific supportive text notes that most patients exhibit congestion without overt hypoperfusion, that mismatches between right- and left-sided filling pressures can impede decongestion, and that disproportionate filling pressures may manifest as dyspnea.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Assessment of Patients Hospitalized With Decompensated HF

rows.recommendation: In patients hospitalized with HF, severity of congestion and adequacy of perfusion should be assessed to guide triage and initial therapy (1-5).
In patients hospitalized with HF, the common precipitating factors and the overall patient trajectory should be assessed to guide appropriate therapy (5,6).
For patients admitted with HF, treatment should address reversible factors, establish optimal volume status, and advance GDMT toward targets for outpatient therapy (6).

section_headings: 9.2. Maintenance or Optimization of GDMT During Hospitalization
content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of acute HF assessment, including signs such as jugular venous distention and edema, elevated natriuretic peptides with variable utility in settings like obesity and sepsis, resting hypoperfusion indicators, and focused hemodynamic evaluation. It addresses assessment of arrhythmias and device therapy, emphasizes hospitalization as a sentinel event to identify precipitants, comorbidities, and optimize hemodynamics and volume status, and highlights reducing residual congestion to lower rehospitalization risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Maintenance or Optimization of GDMT During Hospitalization

rows.recommendation: In patients with HFrEF requiring hospitalization, preexisting GDMT should be continued and optimized to improve outcomes, unless contraindicated (1–5).
In patients experiencing mild decrease of renal function or asymptomatic reduction of blood pressure during HF hospitalization, diuresis and other GDMT should not routinely be discontinued (6–11).
In patients with HFrEF, GDMT should be initiated during hospitalization after clinical stability is achieved (2,3,5,12–18).
In patients with HFrEF, if discontinuation of GDMT is necessary during hospitalization, it should be reinitiated and further optimized as soon as possible (19–22).

content.title: Recommendations for Diuretics in Hospitalized Patients: Decongestion Strategy
section_headings: 9.3. Diuretics in Hospitalized Patients: Decongestion Strategy
content.narrative_summary: The synopsis explains that intravenous loop diuretic therapy provides the most rapid and effective decongestion for hospitalized heart failure patients. Achieving effective diuresis may require doubling initial doses, adding a thiazide diuretic, or adding an MRA to enhance cardiovascular benefits. Persistent congestion at discharge is linked to higher rehospitalization and mortality rates, so loop diuretics at discharge are important to prevent symptom recurrence. Monitoring includes daily fluid intake/output, vital signs, weight, clinical signs of congestion and hypoperfusion, and laboratory tests of electrolytes, urea nitrogen, and creatinine. Evidence from RCTs supports intravenous diuretic protocols without placebo arms, and no RCTs compare intravenous diuretics to placebo.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diuretics in Hospitalized Patients: Decongestion Strategy

rows.recommendation: 1. Patients with HF admitted with evidence of significant fluid overload should be promptly treated with intravenous loop diuretics to improve symptoms and reduce morbidity (1).

2. For patients hospitalized with HF, therapy with diuretics and other guideline-directed medications should be titrated with a goal to resolve clinical evidence of congestion to reduce symptoms and rehospitalizations (1–6).
3. For patients requiring diuretic treatment during hospitalization for HF, the discharge regimen should include a plan for adjustment of diuretics to decrease rehospitalizations (7).

4. In patients hospitalized with HF when diuresis is inadequate to relieve symptoms and signs of congestion, it is reasonable to intensify the diuretic regimen using either: a. higher doses of intravenous loop diuretics (1,3); or b. addition of a second diuretic (3).

content.narrative_summary: Cardiogenic shock is characterized by critically reduced cardiac output leading to end-organ dysfunction, often manifesting as SBP <90 mm Hg and signs of hypoperfusion. Etiologies include acute decompensation of chronic heart failure, acute myocardial infarction without preceding HF, and post–cardiac arrest. Early recognition with invasive hemodynamic assessment, pharmacologic therapy, and temporary mechanical circulatory support aim to optimize perfusion and prevent complications. Evidence is largely retrospective and limited by small, open-label trials. Intravenous inotropes may improve output and hemodynamics, but few prospective data exist to guide agent selection, which is generally driven by clinician familiarity and patient response.

recommendation_tables.title: (continued)

rows.recommendation: In patients with cardiogenic shock, management by a multidisciplinary team experienced in shock is reasonable (17–22).
In patients presenting with cardiogenic shock, placement of a PA line may be considered to define hemodynamic subsets and appropriate management strategies (23–27).
For patients who are not rapidly responding to initial shock measures, triage to centers that can provide temporary MCS may be considered to optimize management (17–22).

content.title: 9.6. Integration of Care: Transitions and Team-Based Approaches
section_headings: 9.6. Integration of Care: Transitions and Team-Based Approaches
content.narrative_summary: The page begins with narrative on escalating support in cardiogenic shock, then presents recommendations for transitions of care. The synopsis highlights that transitions from inpatient to outpatient care in heart failure are vulnerable due to disease progression, complex regimens, comorbidities, and multiple providers, placing patients at high risk for early readmission. Optimal transitional systems—featuring multidisciplinary communication, systematic use and monitoring of guideline-directed medical therapy, medication reconciliation, and thorough documentation—can reduce avoidable readmissions and improve patient satisfaction. The recommendation-specific text for disease management programs notes involvement of cardiologists, primary care clinicians, HF nurses, pharmacists, dietitians, social workers, and community health workers; a Cochrane review of RCTs found that case management or multidisciplinary approaches may decrease all-cause mortality and rehospitalization. Such programs may include education, self-management, medication optimization, device management, weight monitoring, exercise and dietary advice, and facilitated access to care during post-discharge episodes.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Integration of Care: Transitions and Team-Based Approaches

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with high-risk HF, particularly those with recurrent hospitalizations for HFrEF, referral to multidisciplinary HF disease management programs is recommended to reduce the risk of hospitalization (1–4).
2. In patients hospitalized with worsening HF, patient-centered discharge instructions with a clear plan for transitional care should be provided before hospital discharge (5,6).

3. In patients hospitalized with worsening HF, participation in systems that allow benchmarking to performance measures is reasonable to increase use of evidence-based therapy, and to improve quality of care (7–10).

section_headings: 10.1. Management of Comorbidities in Patients With HF
content.narrative_summary: Multimorbidity is common in patients with heart failure, with over 85% having two or more chronic conditions such as hypertension, ischemic heart disease, diabetes, anemia, CKD, morbid obesity, frailty, and malnutrition, which complicate management and prognosis. Specific evidence for therapies addressing depression and CKD in HF is limited. Renal dysfunction increases the risk of toxicity and impairs response to diuretics, and the effectiveness of GDMT in HF patients with concomitant kidney disease is uncertain due to sparse data. The page introduces evolving evidence supporting strategies for managing anemia, hypertension, diabetes, and sleep disorders in HF, and notes that other comorbidities lack large‐scale trial data. Figure 14 is referenced as summarizing COR 1 and 2a recommendations for select HF comorbidities.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the Management of Comorbidities in Patients With HF

rows.recommendation: In patients with HFrEF and iron deficiency with or without anemia, intravenous iron replacement is reasonable to improve functional status and QOL (1-4).
In patients with HF and anemia, erythropoietin-stimulating agents should not be used to improve morbidity and mortality (5,6).
In patients with HFrEF and hypertension, uptitration of GDMT to the maximally tolerated target dose is recommended (7,8).
In patients with HF and suspicion of sleep-disordered breathing, a formal sleep assessment is reasonable to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate between obstructive and central sleep apnea (9,10).
In patients with HF and obstructive sleep apnea, continuous positive airway pressure may be reasonable to improve sleep quality and decrease daytime sleepiness (9,11-13).
In patients with NYHA class II to IV HFrEF and central sleep apnea, adaptive servo-ventilation causes harm (11,12).
In patients with HF and type 2 diabetes, the use of SGLT2i is recommended for the management of hyperglycemia and to reduce HF-related morbidity and mortality (14-17).

content.title: 11. SPECIAL POPULATIONS
content.narrative_summary: This section highlights disparities in HF incidence, risk factors, and outcomes across vulnerable patient populations. It notes the impact of biological factors, social determinants of health, and implicit biases on disease burden and care delivery. Women present with HF later and report lower health status; self-identified Black patients have higher HF incidence, hospitalization, and mortality rates driven primarily by social circumstances. Older adults with HF face multimorbidity, cognitive decline, and frailty. Specific immigrant groups (eg, those exposed to Trypanosoma cruzi) and Southeast Asian and Pacific Islander populations experience unique risks such as Chagas cardiomyopathy and diabetes. Social and medical vulnerabilities—including low income, social isolation, homelessness, substance use, food insecurity, and transportation barriers—impede delivery of guideline-directed medical therapy, particularly in nursing home residents and elderly inpatients. The narrative emphasizes the need for implicit bias training, diverse workforce recruitment, and broad access to HF care.

figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
Columns: Palliative and Supportive Domains of Care; What Palliative Care Adds to Overall HF Management. Rows:
- High-quality communication: Central to palliative care approaches are communication and patient-caregiver engagement techniques (16).
- Conveyance of prognosis: Palliative care specifically addresses patient and caregiver understanding of disease, treatment, and prognosis. Research suggests that patients tend to overestimate their survival (17) and overestimate the potential benefits of treatment (18). Objective risk models can calibrate expectations, but discussion of uncertainty should accompany prognostic conversations, often summarized as “hope for the best, plan for the worst.”
- Clarifying goals of care: Management of patients with HF as their disease becomes end-stage and death seems near includes decisions about when to discontinue treatments designed primarily to prolong life (e.g., ICD, hospitalization, tube feeding); decisions on when to initiate treatments to reduce pain and suffering that may hasten death (e.g., narcotics); and decisions about the location of death, home services, and hospice care. Exploring patients’ expressed preferences, values, needs, concerns, means and desires through clinician-led discussion can clarify values–treatment concordance and improve medical decision-making (12).
- Shared decision-making: Shared decision-making is a process by which patients and clinicians work together to make optimal health care decisions from medically reasonable options that align with what matters most to patients. Shared decision-making requires: unbiased medical evidence about the risks, benefits, and burdens of each alternative, including no intervention; clinician expertise in communication and tailoring that evidence for individual patients; and patient goals and informed preferences (12).
- Symptom management: Dyspnea, fatigue, pain, nausea, depression, anxiety, and other symptoms of HF refractory to cardiovascular therapies can be partially remediated through palliative and supportive approaches in addition to GDMT (5).
- Caregiver support: Care of the patient with heart failure should extend to their loved ones, including beyond their death, to offer support to families and help them cope with loss.

content.narrative_summary: Footnotes indicate that natriuretic peptide cutoff values may have lower specificity in older patients or those with atrial fibrillation or chronic kidney disease, and that higher cutoff values are recommended for diagnosing heart failure in these groups. Natriuretic peptide cutoffs selected for population screening for pre–heart failure (stage B HF) may be below the 99% reference limits and should be defined according to the population risk. Abbreviations defined include AF, BNP, CKD, GLS, HF, LAVI, LV, LVEF, LVMI, NT-proBNP, PA, RWT, and TR.

• Biomarker: BNP ≥35 pg/mL; NT-proBNP ≥125 pg/mL
